Area.evidence_source: Our findings suggest that pragmatic failure and the inadvertent closing down of the SCE were significant barriers to recognition and positive intervention by families and social networks. Talking about suicide can be face-threatening because of the potential to impose upon autonomy and challenge the public self-image of both interlocutors and because an undesired response during an SCE has the potential to jeopardise the interpersonal relationship. This has implications for offering support which, by communicating respect and validation of the person's threatened social identity, could seek to minimise loss of face for the recipient. However, our analysis also suggests there may be occasions when listeners are too willing to be relieved by a friend, colleague or family member of the obligation to intervene in their mental distress. Furthermore, our data show that more needs to be done to dispel unhelpful myths about suicide talk which can influence the outcome of SCEs and hinder intervention.
